> 道常無名，樸雖小，天下莫能臣也.

Three chapters of prohibition: don't take the world and shape it, don't use force to be strong, don't taste the victory. Once the prohibitions are complete, something has to be handed over — what may be kept.

This chapter hands over one character: 樸, the unworked log.

And its real difficulty is not 守樸. It is four characters in the middle: 始制有名.

A man who says the Dao is forever nameless then says: when ordering begins, there are names. If there is no gate between those two statements, the chapter contradicts itself.

The gate is 知止.

## 樸雖小

樸 is 木素 — raw timber, before the carpenter. Small, and the world cannot make it a subject.

小 and 大 are two measures of the same thing, and the chapter uses both. 樸 is 小: it has no position, no rank, no scale of its own. And precisely because it has no scale, nothing can be measured against it and nothing can subordinate it.

臣 is to make someone a subject — to place them in a hierarchy below you. 莫能臣: there is no handle by which to grab it.

## 侯王若能守之，萬物將自賓

If rulers could keep it, the ten thousand things would 自賓 — arrive as guests.

賓, not 臣. One character's difference, and the relation inverts: 臣 is subordinate, 賓 is honored guest. The things come of their own accord, as guests come to a house that is worth visiting, not as subjects reporting for duty.

This is the whole political program of the chapter in one character: not a hierarchy, a hosting.

## 天地相合，以降甘露，民莫之令而自均

Heaven and earth join and send down sweet dew; the people are not ordered and are equal of themselves.

自均 — equalized without instruction. The distribution happens because the conditions are right, not because someone allocated.

## 始制有名

> 始制有名，名亦既有，夫亦將知止.

When ordering begins, there are names. And once names exist, one must know where to stop.

制 is to cut, to fashion, to institute. 名 is not just a label: in this period a name carries a claim — a rank, a share, an obligation. Naming is distribution.

So the admission is significant: structure requires names, and names are necessary. The Dao being nameless does not mean human order can be nameless.

What the Dao's namelessness means is that no name is final. Every name is a 制 — a cut made for a purpose, at a time, by someone.

## 知止可以不殆

Know where to stop, and you can avoid 殆 — exhaustion, peril, being worn out by your own arrangement.

The failure mode is not naming; it is naming without a terminus. When a name is treated as the thing itself, the structure stops being adjustable, and every later correction has to fight the name.

知止 is the discipline that keeps 名 a tool: the rank is a rank, the category is a category, and both can be revised when the situation changes.

## 譬道之在天下，猶川谷之於江海

The Dao in the world is like streams and valleys to the rivers and the sea.

The image closes the chapter with the same geometry as chapter 66 will: the low place is where everything arrives. Not by force, not by suction — by being lower.

## Why this chapter sits here

After 29, 30, and 31 remove the tools of coercion, 32 says what remains: a source that is unworked, a naming that knows its limit, and a position low enough that things come to it.

That is the positive content the prohibitions were making room for.
